description: We are a creative team from Kazakhstan: storytellers, designers and space enthusiasts. We love turning NASA data into clear, engaging stories and visuals. We are still learning, but we are curious, motivated and ready to work hard all weekend. We are looking for teammates with basic coding or data skills (Python, web development, GIS) to help us turn our ideas into a working prototype. Beginners are welcome!
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D museum of NASA hardware left behind on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Every mission leaves something behind: lunar landing stages, rovers that fell silent, and probes drifting beyond the planets. These objects hold decades of engineering history, yet most people never see them. Our project brings them together in one virtual exhibition that anyone can explore from a browser.

Designed for school-age space enthusiasts, the museum turns passive reading into discovery. Visitors move through 3D scenes, examine each piece of hardware up close, and learn where it was left, which mission delivered it, and why it matters. Built on NASA mission data, it makes space history accessible and engaging.

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers by showing that exploration does not end when a mission does. These machines are abandoned, but they are not forgotten.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D museum of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Users explore a virtual exhibition in the browser, with no installation needed. They move between three zones (the Moon, Mars, and deep space), select an object such as a lunar descent stage, a silent rover, or a retired probe, and view it in 3D. Each artifact comes with a short, student-friendly explanation: which mission delivered it, where it was left, what it did, and why it matters. [Describe the navigation: e.g. orbit/zoom controls, clickable hotspots, info panels.]

What are the benefits?

  • Makes space history visual and hands-on instead of text-heavy.
  • Free and open to anyone with a browser, including on school computers [and mobile devices, if true].
  • Gathers scattered mission information about left-behind hardware in one place.
  • Written for school-age learners, so complex engineering is explained simply.

What is the expected impact?

We want to inspire curiosity about space exploration and engineering in young people. The museum can serve as a classroom resource for teachers and a self-guided learning tool for students. It also raises awareness that every mission leaves a legacy: the hardware stays on other worlds long after the mission ends, and it is part of our shared history. [Optional: mention future plans, such as more missions, languages, or quizzes.]

Tools, languages, hardware and software used

  • Front end: [HTML, CSS, JavaScript / TypeScript]
  • 3D graphics: [Three.js / WebGL / React Three Fiber, or your engine]
  • 3D models: [NASA 3D Resources models / Blender / other]
  • Data: [NASA mission data and public sources you used, e.g. NASA APIs, mission archives]
  • Hosting and deployment: Vercel
  • Development tools: [GitHub, VS Code, AI tools if used]

What is creative about the approach?

Most space projects celebrate what NASA sends up and brings back. We tell the opposite story: the machines that stay behind. Presenting them as a museum, with exhibits, zones and “visiting” instead of a database or a list, turns dry mission data into an emotional experience. The title itself carries the idea: these machines are abandoned, but they are not forgotten.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Audience: school-age users, so clear language, simple navigation, and no prior knowledge required.
  • Accessibility: works in a browser, with light enough 3D models to load on ordinary devices [adjust if you optimized specifically].
  • Accuracy: information is based on official NASA sources [confirm].
  • Engagement: interactivity over reading, and a clear story structure (Moon → Mars → deep space).
  • Scalability: the structure allows new artifacts and missions to be added easily.
